newsitem.title: USA: TCI raises customer rates nationwide.
newsitem.headline: TCI raises customer rates nationwide.

text.p: Tele-Communications Inc. on said Thursday it raised its rates by up to 7 percent despite heated competition from the direct broadcast industry.
TCI said the higher rates will take effect in June for 11 million of its 14 million customers, averaging $1.72, or 6.8 percent, a month. The current average rate is $25.33.
TCI attributed 60 percent of the latest hike to rising programming costs.
But the hike is sharply below the 12 percent to 13 percent rate increase rise in 1996.
"There's a big different between 12-13 percent and a 7 percent rate increase. It's more palatable," said James Jungjohann, an analyst with A.G. Edward.

Last year when TCI implemented its large rise it saw customers walk away into the arms of the new DBS industry, but it vows to do a better job this year of explaining to customers the higher costs it faces.
Jungjohann does not see DBS inflicting the same damage this year and notes that DBS growth, while still strong, is slowing.
Nevertheless he expects DBS to have about 10 million customers by 1999, up from just under five million today.

TCI does not disclose the cost of programming, which is proprietary, but Bob Thomson, a senior vice president and spokesman, said, the cost for general cable and sports programming increased by 21.1 percent in 1996, a figure that compared with an increase of 11.9 percent four years earlier.
"It's the most important element of our wholesale cost structure," Thomson told a teleconference call.

Michael Luftman, spokesman for Time Warner Inc.'s Time Warner cable said his company raised rates in January between 5 percent and 10 percent, with the average customer bill going up more than $2 a month.
Luftman said the entire cable industry, even companies aligned with programmers, face pressure from rising programming costs.

At negotiation time, important programmers always bring up their new channels they want to see offered on cable systems, Thomson said. Pressure, he notes, gets tougher as programming improves from the earlier days of "tractor pulling contests on ESPN."
